key_terms.meaning: Uniform Resource Locator — the address of a resource, written as scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment, e.g. https://example.com/books?id=7
A number that identifies one machine on a network, e.g. 142.250.183.4 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::1 (IPv6)
Domain Name System — the distributed service that translates a human name like example.com into an IP address
Top-level domain — the last label of a name, such as .com, .in or .org
A DNS record that maps a name to an IPv6 address; the A record does the same for IPv4
A DNS record that says 'this name is an alias of that name', so the lookup continues at the target name
Mail Exchange record — names the mail servers that accept email for a domain, with a priority number
Time to live — how many seconds a DNS answer may be cached before it must be asked again
The server that holds the real, final records for a domain and answers for it
Small chunks a message is cut into for travel; each carries a header with source and destination addresses
Devices that read a packet's destination address and forward it towards that network, hop by hop
One program (client) asks, another (server) answers; the client starts every exchange
Client tier, server/application tier and data tier, each built and scaled separately
The tier that runs business logic, talks to databases and middleware, and returns results to the web server
Each HTTP request carries all the information needed; the server keeps no memory of earlier requests
The verb in a request line (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE…) that states the action wanted on the resource
A method is safe if it only reads and does not change server state; GET and HEAD are safe
Repeating the same request gives the same server state as sending it once; GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent, POST is not
One TCP connection reused for several HTTP request-response pairs instead of opening a new one each time
A protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a two-way, always-open channel between browser and server
Web Real-Time Communication — browser APIs for direct audio, video and data streams between peers
A developer who can work on the front end, the back end and the database of one application
A stack of MongoDB (database), Express (server framework), React (front end) and Node.js (JavaScript runtime)
A version control system that records snapshots of your files so you can compare, undo and share changes

takeaways: Every web page begins with a name-to-address lookup in DNS, then a connection, then one HTTP request and one response.
DNS answers are cached for their TTL, which is why a changed record takes time to reach everyone.
Splitting a system into client, application and data tiers lets each tier be scaled, tested and replaced on its own.
A web server serves files and forwards dynamic work; an application server holds the business logic and talks to the database.
HTTP is stateless, so state such as a login is carried by cookies or tokens, not by the server remembering you.
HTTPS is ordinary HTTP inside a TLS tunnel, so the methods and status codes are unchanged but the bytes are encrypted.
GET is safe and idempotent, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is neither — this decides when a retry is harmless.
MERN uses one language, JavaScript, from the browser to the server, which is why it is popular for teaching full stack work.
The edit-run-inspect loop — VS Code, Git, browser console and network tab — is where most real debugging happens.
bank_note: Long answers here usually trace one request end to end and then justify a design choice, so practise writing the DNS, connection, HTTP and tier steps in order, with the reason for each.

bank.q: Explain step by step what happens from the moment a user types https://example.com/books into a browser until the page is displayed. Name the role of DNS, IP addresses, TCP and HTTP at each step.
outline: Browser parses the URL: scheme https, host example.com, path /books
Resolver queries DNS; cached answer or full lookup ending at an authoritative nameserver
Client gets an IP address and opens a TCP connection to port 443, then a TLS handshake
Browser sends GET /books with headers; server returns a status code, headers and body
Browser parses HTML, requests sub-resources such as CSS, images and scripts, then renders

bank.q: Describe the DNS record types A, AAAA, CNAME and MX. What does the TTL of a record control, and why does it matter when a record is changed?
outline: A maps a name to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6
CNAME makes one name an alias of another and the lookup continues
MX lists mail servers with a priority value
TTL is the cache lifetime in seconds; long TTL means slow propagation of changes
Caching reduces lookup traffic and latency

bank.q: Distinguish between the Internet and the World Wide Web. Where do packets and routers fit, and what does a browser add on top?
outline: Internet is the network of networks and the addressing and transport that carry packets
WWW is a service on top: resources identified by URLs and fetched with HTTP
Packets are chunks with source and destination addresses; routers forward them hop by hop
Browser is the client that resolves names, requests resources and renders pages

bank.q: Explain client-server and multi-tier web architecture with a diagram. Give one advantage of each extra tier.
outline: Client sends requests, server answers, data tier stores state
Two-tier keeps logic in the client; three-tier adds an application tier
Separate scaling: add web servers without changing the database
Replaceable parts, better security because the database is not exposed
Cost and complexity increase with more tiers

bank.q: Define stateless, safe and idempotent for HTTP, with one example method for each property.
outline: Stateless: no memory of earlier requests; cookies and tokens carry state
Safe: read-only; GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Idempotent: repeat gives same state; GET, PUT, DELETE
POST is neither safe nor idempotent, so retrying it can create duplicates

bank.q: A student submits a login form. Write the HTTP request and the possible responses, showing method, path, headers and status codes. Explain why the form uses POST and not GET.
outline: POST /login HTTP/1.1 with Host, Content-Type, Content-Length, body with credentials
200 or 303 on success; 401 for bad credentials; 400 for a malformed body
GET would put the password in the URL, where it lands in history, logs and Referer headers
POST is not idempotent, which is correct for an action that creates a session

bank.q: Compare the role of a web server and an application server in handling a request for /api/orders. Show which one handles a request for a static image and which one handles the API call.
outline: Web server: terminates HTTP, serves static files directly, forwards dynamic paths
Application server: runs business logic, validates input, queries the database, builds JSON
Static image served by the web server with a cache header; /api/orders goes to the application tier
Middleware such as authentication and logging sits between them

bank.q: You must build a 'list all products' feature in the MERN stack. Describe the file or component you would touch in each of the four parts and the data that passes between them.
outline: MongoDB collection products with fields id, name, price
Express route GET /api/products with a handler that reads from the model
Node.js runs the Express server; JSON travels over HTTP
React component fetches with fetch or axios and renders a list; loading and error states
CORS, port numbers and JSON parsing are the usual student errors

bank.q: A button on your page does nothing when clicked. Explain how you would use VS Code, Git and the browser console and network tab to find and fix the problem.
outline: Console shows JavaScript errors with file and line number
Network tab shows failed requests and status codes
Sources tab lets you set breakpoints and watch variables
Fix in VS Code, then commit the change in Git with a clear message
Never debug on production data; use a branch

bank.q: Users report that a site is slow. Analyse the possible causes across DNS, network, web server, application server and database tiers, and say what you would measure to tell them apart.
outline: DNS: slow or missing cache, wrong TTL
Network: high round-trip time, no persistent connections, large payloads
Web server: no compression or caching, too few workers
Application server: slow business logic, synchronous blocking calls
Database: missing index, N+1 queries, full table scans
Measurement: browser network waterfall, server access logs, query timings

bank.q: For a chat application, compare polling, long polling and WebSockets. State which you would choose and why, and what you give up.
outline: Short polling wastes requests and adds delay
Long polling holds the request open but repeats headers each time
WebSocket: one upgraded connection, two-way, low latency; needs server support and connection management
Fallback and reconnection strategy; proxies must allow the upgrade
Choose WebSockets for frequent two-way messages; plain polling is fine for rare updates

bank.q: Design the tiers for an online food delivery application used from mobile browsers. Justify where you place authentication, order logic and payment, and which tier you would scale first.
outline: Client tier: browser and mobile UI, only presentation and input checks
Application tier: authentication, cart, order state machine, payment gateway calls
Data tier: relational or document store for users, restaurants, orders
Scale stateless web and application servers first; keep sessions in a shared store
HTTPS everywhere; never store card data; log and rate-limit

bank.q: Trace one HTTPS request from browser to database and back, marking where DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP and the application tiers act. Explain how HTTPS changes the picture.
outline: DNS resolution to an IP, with caching and TTL
TCP three-way handshake to port 443
TLS handshake verifies the certificate chain and agrees on keys
HTTP request and response travel encrypted; a proxy sees only the destination
Web server forwards to application server, which queries the database
Response returns through the same connection, which is reused if persistent

glossary.def: The full address of a resource on the web, made of a scheme, a host, an optional port, a path, a query and a fragment.
A worldwide distributed database that converts domain names into IP addresses and other records.
A numeric label, IPv4 or IPv6, that identifies a network interface so packets can reach it.
The top-level domain, the last label of a domain name such as .com, .net, .org or .in.
The DNS server your device asks first; it does the chasing through root, TLD and authoritative servers and returns the final answer.
The DNS server that holds the true records for a zone and gives the final answer for it.
The number of seconds a DNS answer may be cached by resolvers and browsers.
A small unit of data with a header holding source and destination addresses, forwarded independently across a network.
A device that forwards packets towards their destination network using routing tables.
The collection of linked resources, addressed by URLs and fetched over HTTP, that a browser displays.
The program that starts a request for a resource, usually a browser.
A program that listens for requests and returns responses or resources.
Software between two tiers that provides common services such as authentication, logging or message queuing.
A design with a client tier, an application or server tier and a data tier, each independently deployable.
The request-response protocol of the web: a client sends a method and URL, the server returns a status code and body.
HTTP carried inside a TLS connection, giving encryption, integrity and proof of the server's identity.
Transport Layer Security, the protocol that encrypts a connection after a certificate-based handshake.
The verb at the start of an HTTP request line stating the action, such as GET, POST, PUT or DELETE.
A three-digit number in the response line telling the result, such as 200 OK, 404 Not Found or 500 Server Error.
A property of HTTP meaning each request is independent and no earlier request is remembered by the protocol.
A property meaning that sending the same request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once.
Keeping one TCP connection open for many HTTP exchanges, saving the cost of repeated handshakes.
A protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent two-way channel for live data.
Browser APIs and protocols for direct real-time audio, video and data transfer between peers.
A JavaScript stack: MongoDB for data, Express for the server framework, React for the interface, Node.js as the runtime.
Someone who can build and debug the front end, the back end and the database parts of one application.
